title: When the Answer Arrives Early
author: The Last Analogue
summary: Drawing on Alasdair MacIntyre's illustration in After Virtue of teaching a bored seven-year-old to play chess for candy, the essay distinguishes 'external goods' (rewards that could be earned any other way) from 'internal goods' (judgment that can only be developed by playing badly, against real resistance, long enough to improve). The author extends this to AI tutors: a tool that always finds the winning move for a learner delivers the external outcome the practice existed to produce, while quietly hollowing out the internal capacity that practice was supposed to build. The piece invokes Ivan Illich's concept of 'disabling tools' — those that serve a capacity while wasting it away — and closes with a meditation on Proust's distinction between voluntary and involuntary memory, arguing that judgment, like the deepest kind of memory, cannot be delivered on demand; it has to be earned by continuing to play.
points: MacIntyre's chess illustration shows that internal goods (real judgment) only emerge after playing 'badly' long enough against real resistance to notice yourself improving.

Institutions corrupt practices in three ways: substitution (swapping an external good for the internal one), frustration (blocking the practitioner from discovering the practice's real value), and injustice.
An AI tutor that always supplies the winning move is a 'substitution' failure: it collects the external outcome while the learner never discovers the internal good underneath.

Ivan Illich's concept of 'disabling tools' — those that serve a capacity while quietly wasting it away, like a car weakening the legs that once carried you — applies directly to always-correct AI tutoring.
The trouble with an answer that arrives too early isn't that it's wrong; it forecloses the version of you who would have had to go and earn it.
quotes: Because the candy was all she was playing for, she had every reason to cheat whenever she could get away with it.
Judgment, on this account, shows up only in someone who has been playing for the wrong reasons long enough to discover the right one.

Institutions corrupt practices through substitution (one good swapped for another), frustration (institutional priorities blocking the practitioner from ever discovering what the practice had to teach them), and injustice
Some tools, he argued, are disabling. They promise to serve a capacity while quietly wasting it away
An AI tutor that always finds the winning move for you is a disabling tool in exactly that sense.
The trouble with an answer that arrives early has nothing to do with whether it’s right. It forecloses the version of you who would have had to go and get it.
